description: The labs that build AI models: the leaders such as OpenAI and Anthropic, newer labs founded since 2023, and labs that publish their models openly, many of them Chinese.

economics.case: Open models trail the best closed ones by [fact:open_lag] on this site's latest reading, and on OpenRouter, a service that routes developers' requests to many models, open models took [fact:open_share] of the tokens among its most used models. The price of a given level of capability falls steeply on the estimate of Epoch, a research group that tracks AI, which this site reads as emerging. Against that, the businesses paying for AI, on the card and bill-payment data of Ramp, a firm that handles companies' spending, are concentrated among few labs, while the developers routing through OpenRouter spread their tokens across many more labs. The labs spend far ahead of their revenue: for OpenAI and Anthropic, a year of revenue at the current pace is well below the equity (money investors paid for shares) each has raised, and this site's last reading for xAI, taken before its merger into SpaceX, was also well below. Those revenue figures come mostly from the labs themselves, and investors value the labs at many times that revenue. The labs are buying their way up the stack, into the layers above them that sit closer to users: this site's acquisition ledger counts [fact:lab_deals_now] deals in the past year by which model and computing firms took companies in the layers above, including OpenAI's purchases of consumer apps and of a firm that installs AI inside companies, and Anthropic's of developer tools. Some labs already reach users directly: Google puts its Gemini model into Search and its apps, OpenAI reaches consumers through ChatGPT, its chat app, and Microsoft, which is not a frontier lab on this site's map, holds rights to OpenAI's models for its own products and has a revenue-share agreement with OpenAI. The strongest case against this site's judgement comes from Giovanni Cattani, an investor at Hummingbird Ventures, a venture capital firm, and before that an analyst at Blackstone, a private-investment firm. In an article he published on X, the social network, in early September 2026, titled 'Nobody is talking seriously about AI demand', he argued that the frontier labs' revenue rests on a few open-ended, long tasks, such as AI research, writing software and trading, where buyers always want the best model and will pay the labs' margins; on work with a natural limit, he argued, cheaper models from outside the frontier, firms that run models for others, and small models tuned to one job win instead. On that view the rent holds for as long as the uses of AI keep spreading into open-ended work.
economics.commoditising: This site judges that answering a well-understood request, the kind a model from a year before could already handle, is a commodity: many labs and open models do it, and it is priced close to the cost of the chips and power that run it. William Nordhaus, an economist who measured how much of the value of new inventions their makers keep as profit, found that it is a small part; most goes to buyers as lower prices and better products. Kenneth Arrow, an economist who studied how markets handle knowledge, argued that information is hard to own because copying it is cheap; a model's behaviour can be observed and partly copied by a rival training on its answers.
economics.converts_if: Labs turn deployments into switching costs: their coding agents, business tools and staff inside customers become part of how firms work, so moving to a rival means rebuilding, not just repointing. Or a lab owns the place users meet AI, as a chat app with a habit behind it, which Helmer would call branding (a buyer pays more for the same thing because of its name) or network economies (the product grows more useful as more people use it). David Teece, an economist who studied why inventors often fail to keep the returns from what they invent, found that the firm holding the complementary assets (the distribution, sales and systems a product needs to reach buyers) often keeps the profit; Google and Meta already hold theirs, and OpenAI and Anthropic are buying theirs. The rent also lasts, without either, if open-ended uses where only the best model will do keep growing faster than bounded ones, the case Giovanni Cattani makes above. Rules could entrench it too: Sayash Kapoor and Arvind Narayanan, computer scientists at Princeton who study what AI can and cannot do, argued that licensing who may build models, combined with limits on sharing them, would leave only a handful of firms able to build the most capable ones; this site reads that as a route to a regulatory rent (a profit protected by a licence rivals cannot get), which would make the lead last.
economics.kill_shot: Labs keeping their price premium and their share of business spending on models that open ones already match, with no growth in deployments or products; or, the other way, business spending spreading across many labs and open models as freely as developers' routed tokens already do.
economics.mechanism: The frontier labs, OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, xAI and Meta, train the most capable AI models: programs trained on huge amounts of text and data to write, reason and carry out tasks. They sell their use by the token (a fragment of a word) and through products such as chat apps and coding tools. David Ricardo, an English economist who asked in 1817 why landlords grew rich when bread grew dear, found that the owner of the scarcest input collects a rent: profit above what it takes to keep a business going, earned because something holds rivals off. Today the scarce input is the best model, and the lab that has it charges for it. This site judges that the rent on a lead is transitional, because open-weight models (whose trained settings, the weights, are published for anyone to run) arrive some months behind, and that it becomes durable only where a lab is woven into how its customers work or owns the place where users meet it.

rival.title: The labs are durable businesses with high margins

economics.stays_scarce: This site judges that the newest model at the frontier stays scarce for as long as it leads, and that training one costs so much in chips and money that only a handful of firms attempt it. Hamilton Helmer, a strategy consultant who studied why some firms keep earning more than their investors could expect elsewhere, found that a lasting advantage is a benefit behind a barrier; the one that clearly applies today is scale economies (the cost of training a model is fixed, so a lab with more users spreads it thinner, and a rival must match the users to match the cost). Switching costs (what a customer would lose by moving to a rival) are emerging, not proven: they exist where a lab's tools are built into a firm's systems, but this site cannot yet measure how often firms use several labs at once, so it does not count them in this group's powers.
economics.title: A frontier lab's lead earns a rent that open models chase within months; it lasts only where the lab is built into its customers' work

economics.case: This site has revenue readings for few of the neolabs. The voice specialist ElevenLabs reports a run-rate (a recent month's revenue scaled up to a year) that rose fast from the end of 2025 to April 2026 and more slowly since, evidence that a specialist off the big labs' path can earn money. For Mistral, a year of revenue at the current pace is well below the equity it has raised, though that gap has narrowed during 2026. The frontier labs' own costs are the hurdle: training at the frontier costs so much that, on this site's reading, even the leading labs' revenue is well below what they have raised. The specialists face a different test: open models trail the best closed ones by only [fact:open_lag], so a new lab's lead in a general model is short-lived, while a specialty in voice, video, robots or science may lie outside what the general labs train for. This site's acquisition ledger counts only purchases of firms in the layers above the models, so it cannot show a neolab being bought, or its leaders hired, by a bigger lab. This site judges which neolabs sit off the big labs' path; it does not measure it.
economics.commoditising: This site judges that a general model from a new lab is commoditising fastest of all: it competes with the frontier labs above it and the open-weight labs below it. Kenneth Arrow, an economist who studied how markets handle knowledge, argued that information is hard to own because copying it is cheap; a research idea, once published or seen in a product, spreads to labs with more chips. William Nordhaus, an economist who measured how much of the value of new inventions their makers keep as profit, found that it is a small part; most goes to buyers.
economics.converts_if: A specialist's product becomes the tool a trade works in, so switching costs (what a customer would lose by moving to a rival) hold customers after the general labs catch up; or its data from customers and experiments passes Hagiu and Wright's tests and becomes a cornered resource, Helmer's term for preferential access to something others need. A general neolab converts only if its different route (a new way to train, or a model that learns after it is released) proves both better and hard to copy.
economics.kill_shot: A lab founded since 2023 taking the lead on general models and holding it while charging for it; or the specialists' niches being matched by the frontier labs' general models, with the specialists' prices falling to the general labs' level.
economics.mechanism: Neolabs are younger AI labs outside the big frontier group, most founded in the last few years and mostly funded by investors before they sell much: Mistral, which publishes the weights (the trained settings) of some of its models, Safe Superintelligence, Thinking Machines Lab, Reflection AI and Periodic Labs among the general and research labs; ElevenLabs, Black Forest Labs and others in voice, images and video; Physical Intelligence and Skild AI in robots. David Ricardo, an English economist who asked in 1817 why landlords grew rich when bread grew dear, found that the owner of the scarcest input collects a rent: profit above what it takes to keep a business going, earned because something holds rivals off. For a new lab the scarce input is its researchers and its bet on a route the big labs are not taking. This site judges that where that route leads somewhere the frontier labs are heading anyway, the new lab competes with them for chips and money on worse terms, and its people are worth more to a big lab than its business is to investors.

rival.title: The lead among labs keeps changing hands

economics.stays_scarce: This site judges that what stays scarce is the small number of researchers who can lead a frontier training run (the training of the most capable model of its time), and in the specialties, the data and tuning for one kind of work (a voice, a robot's movements, a laboratory's experiments) that general labs have not collected. Andrei Hagiu and Julian Wright, economists who asked when learning from customers' data keeps rivals out, found it does so only when the data is proprietary, keeps its value and improves the product for every customer; a specialty that passes those tests may hold. Hamilton Helmer, a strategy consultant who studied why some firms keep earning more than their investors could expect elsewhere, found that a lasting advantage is a benefit behind a barrier; this site finds no such power proven in the neolabs today.
economics.title: A new lab earns a rent only where its specialty lies off the big labs' path; elsewhere its asset is its people

economics.case: These readings cover all open models, including Meta's and Mistral's, not only this group's. Open models trail the best closed ones by [fact:open_lag] on this site's latest reading, and on OpenRouter, a service that routes developers' requests to many models, they took [fact:open_share] of the tokens among its most used models, though OpenRouter's users lean towards cheap models and firms that buy from the labs directly never appear there. This site reads the open models' gap to the closed frontier on Epoch's capability index (a score from Epoch, a research group that tracks AI, combining many tests of what a model can do) as unclear: it moves both ways between readings. The labs' finances differ: for MiniMax and Zhipu, a year of revenue at the current pace now exceeds what they raised in their share listings, the only rounds this site records for them; for DeepSeek it is far below.
economics.commoditising: The open model is a commodity by design: many hosts serve the same weights and compete on price, so the price of running it falls towards the cost of the chips and power. William Nordhaus, an economist who measured how much of the value of new inventions their makers keep as profit, found that it is a small part; most goes to buyers as lower prices and better products. This site judges open-weight labs are the clearest case of it in AI: the buyers and the hosts keep most of what the model is worth.
economics.converts_if: An open-weight lab's parent earns what the lab gives away: a cloud whose customers come for the free model and stay for the services, which David Teece, an economist who studied why inventors often fail to keep the returns from what they invent, would call owning the complementary assets (the hosting, sales and systems a product needs to reach buyers). Or giving the model away becomes counter-positioning in Helmer's sense, a model a closed lab cannot copy without cutting into its own paid business, with the parent collecting the reward.
economics.kill_shot: Closed labs keeping their prices on models that open ones already match, with open models' share of use falling; or an open-weight lab earning a lasting profit on the model itself rather than on hosting, services or a parent.
economics.mechanism: An open-weight lab publishes its model's weights, the trained settings that are the model, so anyone can run it on their own chips or rent it from a host. This site's open-weight labs include DeepSeek, Alibaba's Qwen team, Moonshot, MiniMax, Zhipu and StepFun, all of them Chinese; Meta's Llama models are open too, though this site counts Meta among the frontier labs and Mistral among the new labs. David Ricardo, an English economist who asked in 1817 why landlords grew rich when bread grew dear, found that the owner of the scarcest input collects a rent: profit above what it takes to keep a business going, earned because something holds rivals off. A model anyone can copy is not scarce, so the lab that publishes it collects little rent on it; this site judges that it earns instead through hosting its own model, selling a better closed version, or serving a parent company or state that wants the model to exist.

rival.title: Labs charge for their lead and let buyers go

economics.stays_scarce: This site judges that what stays scarce is the skill to train a model near the frontier on fewer chips, which some of these labs have shown, and the chips themselves, which export rules make harder for Chinese labs to buy. Hamilton Helmer, a strategy consultant who studied why some firms keep earning more than their investors could expect elsewhere, found that a lasting advantage is a benefit behind a barrier; this site finds none proven for the open-weight labs, because a skill that shows up in a published model can be studied and copied.
economics.title: Open-weight labs give the model away, so they keep little of its value but cap what the closed labs can charge

profiles.customers: Advertisers across the world pay for most of Alphabet's revenue, and the filing names no customer large enough to report separately. Google Cloud sells to businesses and developers; the filing says its remaining performance obligations (revenue contracted but not yet recognised) relate primarily to Google Cloud, and that it has a number of large, long-duration commercial agreements. It also says it has made debt and equity investments in companies with which it signed commercial arrangements at or near the same time, and that if such an investment were impaired it might have to reduce the related contracted revenue; the filing does not name those companies. This site's records hold equity investments by Google in Anthropic, which has also signed for Google's TPU capacity. Alphabet enters significant leases with outside data-centre operators, and has given credit backstops (promises to cover a borrower's debts if it defaults) to data-centre entities it does not control.
profiles.disclosure: Drafted by a Claude model, made by Anthropic, which competes with, sells to or buys from companies in this layer; Alex Brogan reviews this profile before it is relied on.
profiles.market: Alphabet sits in two parts of the chain. As a cloud, Google Cloud rents computing, storage and AI services, offering both graphics processors (GPUs) and its own tensor processing units (TPUs, chips Google designs for the maths AI models run on; the filing names Ironwood as its seventh generation), plus Vertex AI, a platform for building on its Gemini models and other companies' models, and Workspace office software. As a frontier lab (a company building the most capable AI models), it develops the Gemini models, which the filing says run across all of its largest consumer products, including Search through AI Overviews and AI Mode. The filing says the cost of developing its general AI models sits in Alphabet-wide costs rather than in the Google Cloud segment, and that cloud margins are generally lower than advertising margins. It spent heavily on capital (buildings and equipment) in 2025 and said it expected to raise that spending significantly in 2026. This site's filed figures show the Google Cloud operating margin (the share of sales left after running costs) rising sharply over the past year from the lowest among the big clouds. This site judges its market is both renting AI computing and selling AI inside its most widely used consumer products, and that owning chips, models and distribution together is rare.
must_be_true: Gemini stays among the most capable models, so Alphabet does not have to pay another lab for the models that run its own products.
AI answers in Search keep earning at least what the old results page earned, so the advertising that pays for the build-out holds.
TPUs stay competitive with NVIDIA's chips generation after generation, and outside customers keep choosing them, turning a cost advantage into a cloud business.
The Google Cloud margin keeps rising as the contracted backlog turns into revenue, even as the filing warns that cloud margins are lower than advertising's.
Companies it invested in and also sells cloud services to stay solvent and pay, and the credit backstops it has given to data-centre entities are not called.
Its capital spending earns back before the equipment ages out; the filing warns that expected technology advances could change the period over which it benefits from these assets.
profiles.name: Alphabet Inc.

powers.why: One infrastructure serves Search, YouTube, Gemini and Google Cloud; this site judges the benefit is a lower cost for each unit of AI computing, and the barrier is the volume across its consumer products that a cloud-only rival does not have.

Process power is a way of working that takes rivals years to learn. It has designed TPUs through generation after generation alongside its own models, and the filing says it focuses on driving efficiency in its data centres; this site judges that designing chips and models together drives part of that efficiency, that the benefit is AI computing that depends less on buying NVIDIA's chips, and that the barrier is the years of joint chip, software and model work a rival would have to repeat.

rent.reads: a monopoly-like profit, kept by the company itself

would_disprove: The Google Cloud operating margin in this site's filed figures turning down while capital spending keeps rising.
A payment under one of its data-centre credit backstops, or a cut to contracted revenue after an impaired investment.
Large TPU customers moving their next generation of work back to GPUs.
Search revenue falling while more answers are given by AI, showing the answers earn less than the links they replace.
Gemini falling well behind rival models for several model generations in a row.

profiles.customers: Consumers, most directly through ChatGPT, businesses and developers, plus other large companies that build on its models: Amazon will tailor OpenAI models for its own customer-facing apps. Microsoft keeps rights to OpenAI's models and products into the 2030s, and a revenue-share agreement between the two stays in place until an expert panel confirms that OpenAI has reached artificial general intelligence (AI that matches people across most work). API products OpenAI builds with third parties must run on Microsoft's Azure cloud, while its other products may run on any cloud. The sources name no revenue share by customer; this site judges the base is broad, with a direct line to consumers through ChatGPT, but that Microsoft and Amazon stand between OpenAI and many business buyers.
profiles.disclosure: Drafted by a Claude model, made by Anthropic, which competes with, sells to or buys from companies in this layer; Alex Brogan reviews this profile before it is relied on.
profiles.market: OpenAI builds frontier models (the most capable AI systems of their time, trained on huge amounts of text and computing power) and sells them as products people and firms use directly, above all ChatGPT, its chat app, for which this site's records hold a very large weekly user count reported by OpenAI, and through an API (a connection that lets other companies' software send requests to the model and pay per use). Running a model to answer a request is called inference. OpenAI is now a public benefit corporation, or PBC (a for-profit company whose charter also commits it to a stated public purpose), and Microsoft, its long-standing investor, holds a large minority stake after the 2025 recapitalisation (a reorganisation of who owns the company). Its newer deals push toward selling whole systems to businesses: with Amazon it is building a runtime (the software layer an AI agent works inside, keeping memory of prior work and access to a firm's tools and data) for Amazon's cloud customers, and Amazon's cloud is the only outside cloud allowed to resell Frontier, its platform for running teams of AI agents inside a company. Microsoft may now pursue the most advanced AI on its own or with others, and OpenAI may now release open-weight models (models whose trained settings are published so anyone can run them) that meet capability criteria the agreement sets. This site's recorded revenue run-rate (the latest month's revenue scaled up to a full year) for OpenAI has grown steeply but in mid-2026 sat below Anthropic's. Run-rate figures are self-reported: the labs publish them or are the source behind press reports of them, and this profile rests on company and partner announcements, not audited filings. How big the market becomes depends on whether businesses pay for systems built around a model or only for the cheapest model that is good enough.
must_be_true: Revenue grows into its compute commitments (contracts to buy computing power for years ahead): it has contracted for a large further block of Azure services from Microsoft; agreed to deploy AMD's chips across several generations, receiving a warrant (a right to buy AMD shares) tied to those purchases; expanded its multi-year Amazon agreement to cover gigawatts of Amazon's own Trainium chips (Amazon's in-house AI chips; a gigawatt is a very large amount of electric power, about what a big power station produces); and signed multi-year contracts with CoreWeave (a neocloud, a newer firm that rents out AI chips). This site's records also hold a press-reported agreement to buy computing from Oracle, and guarantees from NVIDIA for part of a data-centre build leased to OpenAI. Revenue must rise at least as fast as these bills fall due.

Its prices and margins hold even though open-weight models trail the best closed models by months; this site's estimate of OpenAI's gross margin (revenue left after the direct cost of serving it) fell between 2024 and 2025.
Businesses that build agents on Frontier or the Amazon runtime find it costly to move them, so the deployment, not the model, keeps the customer.

OpenAI, rather than Microsoft or Amazon, owns the relationship with business customers, even though Microsoft keeps rights to its models and a revenue-share agreement, and Amazon resells its platform.
Its direct reach to consumers through ChatGPT, which OpenAI reports and this site cannot check, lasts and turns into paying use; a rival that matches ChatGPT reaches those users directly.

It can keep raising money without leaning further on the cloud and chip suppliers that are also its investors, Microsoft, Amazon and NVIDIA among them, because this site's record shows its revenue run-rate still below the equity (money investors paid for shares) it has raised.
profiles.name: OpenAI

powers.why: Emerging, not proven. This site judges that the cost of training a frontier model is spread over every customer, and the site's venture data show only a few labs raising enough to keep training at the frontier; the barrier holds against newcomers but not against the other frontier labs, and it thins as open-weight models trail by months, not years.

Emerging, not proven. Its agent platform and the runtime with Amazon are built to hold a company's context, tools and permissions, which a customer would have to rebuild to move; this site has no measure yet of customers staying for that reason.

rent.reads: a thin profit, kept by platforms

profiles.customers: Mostly businesses and developers. It says most of the very largest US companies by revenue are customers, that the count of customers spending heavily with it has grown sharply, that firms which start with one use tend to widen it, and that enterprise use makes up most of Claude Code's revenue. It says Claude is sold through the three largest clouds, which also sell rival models, including Amazon's own Nova models and the models Alphabet develops; this site judges that part of its business arrives that way. The sources name no revenue share by customer; this site judges the base is moderately concentrated in large firms and in coding.
profiles.disclosure: Drafted by a Claude model, made by Anthropic, which competes with, sells to or buys from companies in this layer; Alex Brogan reviews this profile before it is relied on.
profiles.market: Anthropic builds frontier models (the most capable AI systems of their time), the Claude family, and sells them to businesses and developers through an API (a connection other software uses to send requests and pay per use), through its own apps, and through work tools: Claude Code, which writes and edits software, and Cowork, which brings Claude Code's abilities to other office work. Running a model to answer a request is called inference. It is a public benefit corporation, or PBC (a for-profit company whose charter also commits it to a stated public purpose). It calls itself the market leader in enterprise AI and coding; that is its own description. It says Claude is sold on the largest clouds, Amazon's, Google's and Microsoft's, and runs on Amazon's Trainium chips (Amazon's in-house AI chips), Google's TPUs (Google's in-house AI chips) and NVIDIA's GPUs (graphics processing units, the chips most AI runs on). This site's recorded revenue run-rate (the latest month's revenue scaled up to a full year) for Anthropic has grown steeply and in mid-2026 sat above OpenAI's. Run-rate figures are self-reported: the labs publish them or are the source behind press reports of them, and this profile rests on company and partner announcements, not audited filings. How big the market becomes depends on whether businesses keep paying a premium for its models once cheaper ones are good enough for the same work.
must_be_true: Revenue grows into its compute commitments (contracts to buy computing power for years ahead): in 2026 it signed for gigawatts of new capacity from Amazon and of TPU capacity from Google and Broadcom (a gigawatt is a very large amount of electric power, about what a big power station produces), and for GPU capacity from SpaceX; in November 2025 it chose Fluidstack (a neocloud, a newer firm that rents out AI computing) to build custom data centres for it. This site's records also hold its commitment to buy Azure computing from Microsoft and its commitment to spend on AWS over the next decade. Revenue must rise at least as fast as these bills fall due.

Its prices and margins hold even though open-weight models (models whose trained settings are published so anyone can run them) trail the best closed models by months; this site's gross-margin estimate for Anthropic (revenue left after the direct cost of serving it) sits at about the same level as OpenAI's, which this site judges is well below a typical software firm's.
Businesses that build Claude into their coding and daily work find it costly to move, even though the clouds that resell Claude sell rival models through the same menu.

profiles.market: Periodic Labs builds AI models together with autonomous laboratories (labs where robots run experiments and software decides what to try next), starting with materials science: new superconductors (materials that carry electricity with no loss) and magnets. Its bet is that experiments produce data no one else has, which trains better scientific AI, which picks better experiments. In 2026 it released Neon, a large model it built by mid-training (further broad training on a chosen body of material) and then reinforcement learning (training by rewarding good answers) on its own lab data; it says Neon beats leading general models from OpenAI and Anthropic at one analysis task, reading X-ray diffraction results (patterns that show a material's crystal structure), with relatively little compute (computing power). It also sells to industry, for instance training agents for a chip maker working on heat problems. It is private and early; its backers include Andreessen Horowitz and NVIDIA's venture arm. How big the market becomes depends on whether it makes materials others will pay for, and on who keeps the profit when it does.

profiles.customers: Advertisers pay for substantially all of it, the 10-K says. It also says most of its revenue comes from marketers advertising on Facebook and Instagram, that they make no long-term commitments, and that the loss of marketers or cuts in their spending could seriously harm the business. profiles.market: Meta runs Facebook, Instagram, Messenger, WhatsApp and Threads, and its 10-K (the annual report US companies file with their regulator) says it earns substantially all its revenue from advertising on those apps. Its AI work sits on both sides of that business. It builds its own models, including the Llama family, which it has released openly in the past; the 10-K says it expects to train a mix of open and closed models from here (an open model is one whose trained settings are published so anyone can run it). It offers Meta AI, an assistant available inside its apps, as a stand-alone app, on its AI glasses and on the web. And it uses AI to choose which posts and ads each person sees, which the 10-K credits with better ad targeting and measurement. It states a goal of building superintelligence, which it defines as AI that surpasses human intelligence. To pay for this it spends heavily on data centres: this site's records from its filings show its capital spending (money spent on buildings and machines) growing much faster than its revenue in 2025 and again so far in 2026, and its 10-K lists large commitments, mostly for data centres and for computing capacity rented from other firms. In October 2025 it entered an arrangement to co-develop a data-centre campus in Louisiana, in which it holds a minority interest. In June 2025 it bought a non-voting minority stake in Scale AI, a seller of training data made by people; its filings say it has no significant influence over Scale's operations, and Scale's founder joined Meta to work on its AI. This site's records also hold Meta buying Manus and Limitless in December 2025 and Stilla in September 2026, and buying or hiring teams from other small AI firms in March 2026. The question is whether AI adds to or eats into the advertising business that pays for it.
must_be_true: Advertising keeps paying for the AI build-out. The 10-K says its AI work will need more spending on infrastructure and staff, and this site's records show capital spending rising far faster than revenue; ad revenue must keep growing fast enough to carry those costs and the losses of Reality Labs, its glasses and headsets division, which the 10-K says depends on profits earned elsewhere.

AI keeps making its ads work better, so advertisers keep paying more per ad; the 10-K reports more ads shown and a higher average price per ad in 2025, and credits its AI with better targeting and measurement.

People keep turning to Meta AI inside apps they already use rather than moving their questions, shopping and time to assistants from OpenAI or Google. William Nordhaus, an economist who measured how much of the value of new inventions their makers keep, found that most goes to users; this site judges a free assistant only pays Meta if the attention it holds can be sold to advertisers.
Its own models stay close enough to the best to power its products, so it need not pay rival labs for the capability; the 10-K lists competitors whose AI may be better or cheaper among its risks.

Regulators let it keep showing personalised ads. The 10-K says the European Commission ruled in April 2025 that its offer of a paid subscription with no ads did not comply with EU rules, a decision it has appealed.

Its minority stake in Scale AI, which carries no vote, and its purchases of small AI firms add skills and products without drawing new limits from competition authorities, whose past scrutiny of its acquisitions the 10-K describes.

powers.why: Hamilton Helmer, a strategy consultant who studied why some firms keep earning more than their rivals, found that a lasting advantage needs both a benefit and a barrier to copying. In Meta's social apps the benefit is that each user makes the apps more useful to friends and more valuable to advertisers; the barrier is that a rival must assemble a comparable audience first. The 10-K shows the audience still growing in 2025, with more ads shown and a higher average price per ad, so this site counts the power proven in its social apps. It finds no evidence yet that the power extends to Meta AI itself, where one person's chat does not improve another's.

Emerging, not proven: this site judges that the cost of training models and building ad-ranking systems is spread over Meta's very large audience and ad sales, so each user costs it less than a smaller rival; but the barrier holds only against newcomers, not against Google or the frontier labs (the firms building the most capable AI systems), which spend at similar scale and are its main AI rivals.

Emerging, not proven: counter-positioning is a newcomer's model the incumbent could copy only by damaging its own business. The benefit is that Meta can give AI away inside its apps and let advertising pay; the barrier is that a lab living on subscriptions and paid access to its models would give up that revenue by doing the same. But the labs can add advertising too, and Meta AI has no revenue the 10-K reports, so this site does not count the barrier as proven.
